description: Places where Vattel, defending Leibniz and Wolff, answers a question of the Théodicée or the Psychologia rationalis differently. Pairs from the units that reuse these sources, screened by Claude Sonnet (DEF41_DIV_SCREEN_PROMPT.md), kept or rejected by Claude Opus (DEF41_DIV_VERIFY_PROMPT.md). relation: diverges or partly. severity: 3 incompatible answers, 2 different ground or a changed scope, 1 a qualification. Disagreements with Crousaz and Roques are in the reuse rows (stance rejects). Machine judgements, not checked by hand.

items.question: Whether Leibniz approves Origen's universal salvation
items.comment: Leibniz, Théod. § 17, reports that pious, learned and bold persons have revived Origen's view that all rational creatures will finally become blessed. He calls it a great paradox and notes that Le Clerc pleaded for it without declaring for it. Vattel says Leibniz makes it clear enough that he approves Origen's view and offers it as an opening for bolder minds.
items.passage: l'Auteur fait assez entendre qu'il approuve le sentiment d'ORIGENES
items.sourcePassage: Plusieurs personnes pieuses et même savantes, mais hardies, ont ressuscité le sentiment d’Origène

items.question: Whether eternal damnation leaves a difficulty for the best world
items.comment: Leibniz, Théod. § 19, holds that even on the established doctrine that the eternally damned far outnumber the saved, evil would appear almost as nothing beside the good of the whole City of God. Vattel quotes this answer and holds that retaining eternal punishment still leaves a difficulty that cannot be fully resolved. He makes the system demonstrative only on a kind of Origenism under which all intelligences reach happiness.
items.passage: Mais il faut avouër qu'en retenant le Dogme de l'éternité des peines , il reste encore quelque embarras, dont il est difficile de se démêler parfaitement
items.sourcePassage: il faut dire que le mal ne laisserait pas de paraître presque comme rien en comparaison du bien, quand on considérera la véritable grandeur de la cité de Dieu

items.question: Whether moral evil is inseparable from every possible world
items.comment: Leibniz, Théod. § 25 holds that God only permits moral evil as a sine qua non, by a hypothetical necessity that binds it to the best. Vattel makes moral evil an inseparable condition of the best world and of any world whatever, because every creature is essentially imperfect. Leibniz ties sin to the choice of the best plan, and in the Abrégé, obj. 1 he grants that a world without evil was possible. Vattel ties sin to creatureliness as such.
items.passage: Dieu a dû le permettre à titre de sine quo non, de condition inséparable du meilleur Monde possible, & même de tout Monde , quel qu'il puisse être
items.sourcePassage: mais qu’il ne veut que permettre le mal moral à titre du sine quo non ou de nécessité hypothétique, qui le lie avec le meilleur

items.question: Whether the laws of force and reaction demonstrate against physical influence
items.comment: Leibniz, Théod. § 346, calls the conservation of force and the equality of action and reaction very plausible suppositions that cannot be demonstrated geometrically and carry no absolute necessity. Vattel calls these laws certain and says they give a demonstration against the system of physical influence. Vattel raises to demonstrative certainty premises that Leibniz treats as plausible principles of a higher philosophy.
items.passage: on a aujourd'hui une Démonstration contre ce système
items.sourcePassage: cet axiome d’une philosophie supérieure ne saurait être démontré géométriquement

items.question: How Descartes met the conservation difficulty
items.comment: Leibniz, Théod. § 60, says Descartes kept a partial influence of the soul on the body: the soul could not change the quantity of motion but could change its direction. Vattel says Descartes and his followers rejected the system of influence for this reason and put occasional causes in its place. On Leibniz's account Descartes himself did not give up influence.
items.passage: c'est pour cela qu'ils ont rejetté le système de l'Influence, & substitué à sa place celui des Causes occasionelles
items.sourcePassage: il a cru que l’âme pourrait pourtant avoir le pouvoir de changer la direction des mouvements qui se font dans le corps

items.question: Whether the soul's rise to reason is natural
items.comment: Leibniz, Théod. § 91, leaves open whether a sensitive soul rises to reason by natural means or by a kind of transcreation, and says he finds the natural means hard to conceive. Vattel judges the natural passage very probable, since confused and distinct ideas are linked and we pass daily from one to the other. The two lean to opposite answers on a question both leave open.
items.passage: Cependant le prémier sentiment paroit fort probable
items.sourcePassage: soit qu’il y ait un moyen naturel d’élever une âme sensitive au degré d’âme raisonnable (ce que j’ai de la peine à concevoir)

items.question: Whether the system needs Origenism to be demonstrative
items.comment: Leibniz, Théod. § 211, says only that an Origenist who holds that all rational creatures will finally become happy will be even easier to satisfy. Vattel holds that Leibniz's system becomes demonstrative only once a kind of Origenism is added, and says Leibniz recognised this. Leibniz treats Origenism as an easier answer for those who already hold it. He does not make the proof depend on it.
items.passage: le système de Mr. DE LEIBNITZ, ne devient démonstratif, qu'en y faisant entrer une espèce d'Origenisme
items.sourcePassage: Un origéniste qui voudra que celles qui sont rationnelles deviennent toutes enfin heureuses, sera encore plus aisé à contenter.

items.question: Whether final approval fixes the will
items.comment: Leibniz, Théod. § 311 distinguishes the effort to act from the judgment, holds that a new perception can suspend or change it, and concludes that the link between judgment and will is not so necessary as one might think. Vattel cites this section for the effort to act but first equates giving final approval with determining oneself. Leibniz leaves a gap between judgment and will that Vattel's equation closes.
items.passage: Or donner son approbation en dernier ressort, c'est la même chose que se déterminer.
items.sourcePassage: Ainsi la liaison entre le jugement et la volonté n’est pas si nécessaire qu’on pourrait penser.

items.question: Whether a little evil is needed to make the good felt
items.comment: Leibniz, Théod. § 12, doubts that health is enjoyed enough without illness and holds that a little evil is most often needed to make the good more sensible, that is, greater. Vattel says Leibniz means only that contrast is an advantage drawn from an evil that arises for other reasons. Vattel's reading drops the claim that the evil is usually required and that it enlarges the good.
items.passage: Il dit seulement, que c'est au moins un avantage, qui se tire d'une maladie, qui arrive par d'autres raisons
items.sourcePassage: Et ne faut-il pas le plus souvent qu’un peu de mal rende le bien plus sensible, c’est-à-dire plus grand ?

items.question: Whether the created soul is ever passive
items.comment: Leibniz, Théod. § 32 defines the creature's action as a modification flowing naturally from its substance, and holds that God alone acts purely, without admixture of what is called being acted upon. Vattel adopts the definition and concludes that everything in the soul is its action, because the soul can never be passive. Leibniz mixes passion into all creaturely action, and Vattel excludes it from the soul.
items.passage: car elle ne peut jamais être passive
items.sourcePassage: Il est vrai que Dieu est le seul dont l’action est pure et sans mélange de ce qu’on appelle pâtir

items.question: When miracles count against occasionalism
items.comment: Wolff, Psych. rat. § 604 holds that so long as natural harmony is not shown possible, it seems not improbable that it cannot be obtained, and the occasionalist is not to be blamed for supposing supernatural modifications. Vattel restates the thesis as a necessity: when an effect cannot be shown to be naturally explicable, one must have recourse to the immediate operation of the First Cause, because there is no other way to explain it. Wolff's excuse rests on probability. Vattel's rests on the absence of any other explanation.
items.passage: parce qu'en pareil Cas, il n'y a point d'autre manière d'expliquer l'effet, dont on cherche la raison
items.sourcePassage: Quamdiu enim ostendi nequit, harmoniam animæ ac corporis per naturam utriusque substantiæ subsistere posse, haud prorsus improbabile videtur id fieri non posse.

items.question: Whether answering the first objection requires the best-world system
items.comment: Leibniz, Théod., Abrégé, obj. 1 denies the major because an evil may be accompanied by a greater good. He states that it suffices to show that a world with evil could be better than one without, and treats the proof that this world is the best as going beyond what the objection requires. Vattel holds that the major cannot be denied without the best-world thesis and the universal connection of things, because without that principle removing evils would always make the world more perfect. The minimal reply Leibniz shares with Augustine and Aquinas becomes in Vattel a reply available only within the Leibnizian system.
items.passage: sans ce Principe, on vous soutiendroit avec raison, que le Monde seroit toujours plus parfait , à proportion que l'on en retrancheroit des maux
items.sourcePassage: Il suffit donc, pour anéantir l’objection, de faire voir qu’un monde avec le mal pouvait être meilleur qu’un monde sans mal
